report.source_text: Repeated capillary blood gases over the next 7 days showed hyponatremia ranging between 121 and 137 mmol/L [normal 135–145 mmol/L], hyperkalemia ranging between 5.5–8.0 mmol/L [normal for age 4.0–6.5 mmol/L] in both mildly hemolyzed and non-hemolyzed samples, and chloride values ranging between 86 and 100 mmol/L [normal 98–107 mmol/L].

clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: Premature female infant with antenatal polyhydramnios presenting with severe dehydration, weight loss, and biochemical evidence of hyponatremia with transient hyperkalemia (5.5-8.0 mmol/L) in the first week. This electrolyte pattern (hyperkalemia rather than hypokalemia) is consistent with neonatal presentation of Bartter syndrome type II (ROMK deficiency), where impaired potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct causes initial hyperkalemia before transitioning to hypokalemia. Pending confirmation of inappropriate renal salt wasting (elevated urinary chloride despite hypovolemia) and genetic confirmation of KCNJ1 variants.

report.source_text: Testing of the urine on day of life 7 revealed an osmolality of 369 mOsm/kg [reference interval in neonates not well established], high sodium of 118 mmol/L [renal salt wasting defined as urinary sodium > 40 mmol/L], low potassium of 7 mmol/L, chloride of 94 mmol/L, and low urine creatinine of 0.3 mmol/L. As there are no established normal urine electrolyte values, these should be interpreted in context with serum values.

report.source_text: Further investigations revealed a normal magnesium level of 0.95 mmol/L [0.65–1.05 mmol/L], an elevated aldosterone of > 27,000 pmol/L [normal 320–4621 pmol/L], and elevated renin at > 3000 ng/L [upper limit of normal 175 ng/L] [8]. The cortisol was 629 nmol/L [133–537 nmol/L], ACTH was 6.6 pmol/L [normal 1.98–12.47 pmol/L], and 17-OHP was mildly elevated at 14.8 nmol/L [normal 0.2–4.7 nmol/L]. These findings were sufficient to rule out congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency.

report.source_text: Results showed two pathogenic variants in the KCNJ1 gene [1]: a paternally inherited frameshift deletion, p.Glu334Glyfs*35 (c.996_999del, exon 5), predicted to result in premature protein termination and previously reported as causative for Bartter syndrome [6], and [2] a maternally inherited missense variant, p. Pro110Leu (c.329C > T, exon 5) (Fig. 2), previously reported to be pathogenic in compound heterozygosity with other pathogenic variants in KCNJ1 [8–10].

report.source_text: The patient required sodium chloride supplementation up to a maximum dose of 7.9 mmol/kg/day included in the total parenteral nutrition, started on day of life 7 to gradually achieve normal sodium levels. A trial of fludrocortisone therapy was recommended by endocrinology to definitively rule out CAH. The patient received two doses given on day 9 (0.03 mg/kg/dose) of life and was without clinical response. The patient’s electrolytes normalized by 4 weeks of life and supplementation was gradually weaned off by 7 weeks of life.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A premature female infant (33+6 weeks, 1450g) with antenatal polyhydramnios presented at birth with severe dehydration (22% weight loss), poor responsiveness requiring non-invasive ventilation, and clinical evidence of renal salt-wasting. Initial workup revealed hyponatremia (121-137 mmol/L) and transient hyperkalemia (5.5-8.0 mmol/L) with inappropriately elevated urinary sodium (118 mmol/L) and low urinary potassium (7 mmol/L), consistent with impaired potassium secretion. Severe secondary hyperaldosteronism was documented (aldosterone >27,000 pmol/L, renin >3000 ng/L). Congenital adrenal hyperplasia was ruled out by normal cortisol, ACTH, and 17-OHP levels and lack of response to fludrocortisone trial. Genetic testing confirmed compound heterozygosity for pathogenic KCNJ1 variants (paternal frameshift p.Glu334Glyfs*35 and maternal missense p.Pro110Leu). The infant was treated with sodium chloride supplementation (up to 7.9 mmol/kg/day), with electrolytes normalizing by 4 weeks and supplementation weaned by 7 weeks. Follow-up at 6 months demonstrated normal acid-base status (pH 7.35, bicarbonate 29 mmol/L), confirming the absence of classic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
